prize_parts.citation: For a visionary Romanian-language oeuvre whose dense, patterned prose turns memory, the body and dream into an encyclopedic metaphysical architecture.

statement.case_for: After reading my colleagues' openings I keep Cărtărescu first, on the criterion of a voice found in this writer's work and nowhere else. The public record for Blinding (the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid shows a voice that is recognizable at sentence level. It is also an architecture in which the intimate, the bodily and the cosmic are joined as a project of intellectual depth, not as stylistic display. The poetic origins of the prose and the long span of the career point to sustained achievement, and a decision would not be premature. The citation scope is clean: one writer, and a Romanian-language prose project that recurs in recognizable form across genres. Adonis remains a very close second on formal and linguistic achievement, because he remade the language of a major poetic tradition. My preference for Cărtărescu rests on how confidently each case can be assessed across the whole oeuvre from the evidence available to this committee. It does not rest on any difference in seriousness between the two.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the claim rests on density, rhythm and syntax in Romanian, and I know the work only through translation and secondary description. Maximalist, self-enclosing systems can repeat their motifs, so equal quality across the whole corpus, including the poetry and early work, is not established. If the committee cannot resolve how much of the prose texture survives translation, the case for the central novels is weaker than it looks. Adonis's case has a parallel weakness, since prosody and intertextuality in Arabic are hard to judge from translated versions.

responses.point: Carlberg places Cărtărescu first but warns that translation coverage is uneven and that the density of the work may make translation quality decisive. She also ranks Zurita third and notes that the non-textual works would need a literary argument.
responses.response: I accept the translation point in full. It is the main uncertainty in my own case, and I cannot resolve it from the supplied evidence, so I would want the committee to test the central claim against the prose itself and not against reputation. On Zurita I agree that any citation would have to rest on the verse sequences, with the landscape and sky works treated as extensions of the poetry. That is why I rank him fifth. The poems' verbal texture is the hardest part to judge from a distance, and I would not move him above Adonis or Cărtărescu on current evidence.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis second on formal and linguistic achievement. He notes that timing arises only through advanced age, which is not a literary criterion, and that political commentary must not stand in for judgment of the poems. He also ranks Kincaid third and recognizes that her oeuvre is modest in size.
responses.response: I agree that age and public visibility are not literary arguments, and that the case for Adonis must rest on the poems and their relation to inherited Arabic forms. Where I would qualify his view is on how much the essays should carry in a citation. I think the verse must stay central, and the critical writing should be named only as part of the same project. I also note that Olsson accepts the limits of a compact oeuvre for Kincaid, who is not on this shortlist. I would apply the same breadth test to Michon, so I do not treat compactness as disqualifying, but I do weigh how much work the whole-oeuvre claim has to bear.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg values Michon's voice and linguistic achievement but ranks him sixth. He sees the depth as concentrated rather than broad, and he asks whether a small corpus supports a prize for the entire oeuvre.
responses.response: This is the objection I take most seriously against my own third-place ranking of Michon. The sentence-level discipline and the concern with vocation, ancestry and the survival of art are very distinctive. But a slim body of work puts real weight on the 'significance across a body of work' criterion, and French syntax is hard to carry into translation. I therefore keep Michon as an alternative and not as my first choice. If the committee judges that intensity can substitute for breadth, my view of him would change. I do not yet think the evidence settles that.

responses.point: Palm ranks Anne Carson second. She finds the formal inventiveness and the intellectual and emotional depth considerable, but she admits that cross-genre work is hard to compare with novel-centered oeuvres under common criteria.
responses.response: I share the comparability problem, and I think it is a reason for caution and not a reason to dismiss her. I rank Carson sixth because the category boundaries between poetry, essay, translation and visual book complicate the assessment of a whole body of work. It is also not yet evident to me that her oeuvre rests on one achievement of the weight that Cărtărescu's or Adonis's does. I would want a precise citation scope before treating her as a first choice.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's Romanian prose rhythm and density survives translation, and how evenly the poetry and early work sustain the quality of the central novels.

How much of Adonis's prosodic, lexical and intertextual achievement in Arabic can be assessed from translations and secondary accounts, and how the poetry and essays should be weighted in one citation.
Whether the slim corpus of Michon can support a whole-oeuvre prize under the breadth criterion.
My assessments rest on public knowledge of the listed works and not on independently verified reading of every text.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile.
